sections.h2: How Michigan property tax is calculated
sections.html:
Michigan assesses property at 50 percent of its true cash value, and that half-value figure is the state equalized value (SEV). Tax is not charged on SEV directly. It is charged on taxable value, which for each parcel is the lesser of two numbers: last year's taxable value (less losses) multiplied by 1.05 or the inflation rate, whichever is smaller, plus additions, or the current SEV (MCL 211.27a).

This is the Proposal A cap. It is why two neighboring houses of equal market value can carry very different bills. A long-time owner usually pays on a taxable value well below SEV, and that cushion goes with the owner, not the parcel. Most sale-day tax surprises in Michigan trace back to this one rule.

  • SEV is half of the assessor's estimate of true cash value.
  • Taxable value grows slowly while the same owner holds the parcel.
  • Each local taxing unit sets a millage rate, and that rate is applied to taxable value to produce the bill.

sections.h2: What happens to taxable value when the house sells
sections.html:
A transfer of ownership resets taxable value. For the calendar year after the transfer, taxable value becomes the SEV, and the 5-percent-or-inflation cap then applies again from that new base (MCL 211.27a(3) and (4)). Transfer is defined broadly. A deed, a land contract, certain trust changes, and a distribution under a will or by intestacy all count.

An heir who is the decedent's spouse, parent, child, sibling or grandchild can take a home without the reset, as long as it stays residential (MCL 211.27a(6)(f)). A land contract counts as a transfer on the day it is signed, so the deed that follows does not trigger a second reset.

The new owner files a State Tax Commission form with the local assessing office. It lists the parties, the date, the real price paid and the parcel number or legal description, and it is due 45 days after the transfer (MCL 211.27a(10)). The register of deeds also passes recorded deeds to the assessor at least monthly, so the reset does not wait on that paperwork.

sections.h2: Board of review and Tax Tribunal appeals
sections.html:
The first stop is the local board of review. It meets the second Monday in March, and a city or township may choose the Tuesday or Wednesday after that as the starting date. The opening session begins no earlier than 9 a.m. and no later than 3 p.m. and runs six hours or more. Across that week the board sits 12 hours, three of them in the evening (MCL 211.30).

An owner or an agent can ask for a corrected assessed or taxable value, and the board must correct it if sufficient cause is shown. A nonresident can protest by letter, and a township or city may allow resident protests by letter too. The board mails its written decision, with a notice about the tribunal, no later than the first Monday of June.

The Michigan Tax Tribunal hears the next level. For a house, the petition goes in by July 31 of the tax year, and the same date covers agricultural and timber-cutover land. Commercial, industrial and developmental real property, plus related personal property, has an earlier May 31 date. Other matters get 35 days from the final decision. A residential valuation case generally starts with a board of review protest. Disputes limited to arithmetic mistakes on a bill get 60 days from the treasurer's mailing (MCL 205.735a).

sections.h2: Principal residence exemption when you sell
sections.html:
The principal residence exemption (PRE) removes the local school operating tax from an owner's home. An owner claims it by filing a Principal Residence Exemption Affidavit, Form 2368, with the city or township assessor. Filing by June 1 lowers the summer levy, and a filing between June 2 and November 1 starts with the winter levy (Treasury PRE claim requirements).

At sale you have to undo it. Once the home is no longer your principal residence, send Form 2602, a Request to Rescind, to the assessor within 90 days. A late filing costs $5 a day, capped at $200, and the exemption comes off the roll at the end of the filing year.

The same duty reaches other situations. After an owner dies, the personal representative or trustee files it. After a divorce, the departing spouse files it. After a lender forecloses, the former borrower files it once the home is vacated. Closing agents, assessors and the Treasury website all hand out the forms.

Township and city treasurers send the bills and collect first. A summer levy is a lien and is due July 1, and interest runs on anything collected after September 14. Whatever is still unpaid on March 1 goes to the county as delinquent (MCL 211.44a).

A collecting unit may add an administration fee of up to 1 percent to a bill paid before mid-February. From February 15 until the delinquent return, the city or township may authorize that fee plus a 3 percent late charge (MCL 211.44).

The serious step comes a year later. Each March 1, parcels that were delinquent for a full prior 12 months forfeit to the county treasurer, and a $175 fee is added. A certificate is recorded at the deeds office within 45 days. To redeem, you pay everything owed plus extra interest of one-half percent a month. Redemption stays open through the March 31 that follows the foreclosure judgment, or 21 days after judgment if the case is contested (MCL 211.78g). A seller with back taxes should ask the county treasurer for a written payoff figure well before then.

Key Michigan property tax dates
StepDate or rule
Board of reviewSecond Monday in March, or the Tuesday or Wednesday after
Tribunal petition, residentialBy July 31 of the tax year
Summer taxDue July 1; interest after September 14
ForfeitureMarch 1 after 12 months or more delinquent
Transfer noticeBuyer tells the assessor within 45 days

Start with the parcel's tax history and work outward. Closing agents ask for these same items, and a gap is cheaper to close early.

  • Ask the township or city treasurer which bills are paid, then ask the county office whether any year went delinquent.
  • Check the exemption status with the assessor, and send in the rescission form within 90 days of moving out.
  • Tell the buyer that taxable value moves up to SEV the year after closing, so last year's bill understates what comes next.
  • To contest the assessment on a house, plan for the March board first and the July 31 tribunal date after it.
  • For an inherited house, find out whether the family exception keeps the old taxable value before the heirs decide whether to keep or sell.

Owners several years behind should act before forfeiture. After it, the parcel sits with the county treasurer, and the foreclosing governmental unit takes possession only on the April 1 after judgment. Redemption ends at the March 31 cutoff.

Back taxes, a lingering exemption or a pending appeal can slow a traditional listing, because a buyer's lender and title company want clean numbers. In a cash sale, a buyer who pays from their own funds does not wait on a lender's underwriting, so the tax payoff can be settled at closing from the proceeds. You still need the written payoff figure from the treasurer, and you still file the rescission form after you move. What a cash sale skips is the repair list, the appraisal and the lender's timeline.

If you are weighing an offer while taxes are owed, line up three things first: the payoff letter, the parcel number from your tax bill, and the date you stopped living in the home. With those in hand the closing agent can show exactly what comes out of the proceeds and what the buyer takes on.

faqs.q: When does the Michigan board of review meet?
faqs.a: The week of the second Monday in March. Some cities and townships open one or two days later, on the Tuesday or Wednesday, and every board owes 12 hours of hearings that week, with three after 6 p.m.

faqs.q: When must a homeowner petition the Michigan Tax Tribunal?
faqs.a: Your petition must be filed by July 31 of the tax year. Residential cases generally begin with a board of review protest. Commercial and industrial real property follow an earlier May 31 date.

faqs.q: Do Michigan property taxes go up when a house is sold?
faqs.a: Often. A transfer of ownership sets taxable value equal to SEV for the next calendar year, wiping out the Proposal A gap the seller built up. The buyer reports the transfer to the assessor within 45 days.

faqs.q: How do I remove the principal residence exemption after selling?
faqs.a: Send Form 2602 to the local assessor within 90 days of ceasing to live there as your principal residence. Missing the window triggers $5 per day, with a $200 ceiling.

faqs.q: When does Michigan property go into forfeiture for unpaid taxes?
faqs.a: Each March 1, after taxes have gone unpaid for the prior 12 months or longer. The parcel is forfeited to the county treasurer for the amount owed, and redemption by full payment stays possible through the following March 31 after the foreclosure judgment.
